definition: An acronym for five object-oriented design principles collected by Robert C. Martin: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion. They are questions to ask when a design is hard to change, not rules to apply everywhere.
example: A class that both calculates pay and saves itself to the database fails the S of SOLID.

definition: The S in SOLID. Robert C. Martin's version: a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor, meaning one group of people who might ask for it to change. Code that changes for different groups' reasons should be split.
example: Pay rules (finance) and hours reports (operations) in one Employee class break SRP.

aliases: open for extension but closed for modification
definition: The O in SOLID, from Bertrand Meyer (1988): software should be open for extension but closed for modification. You add new behaviour by adding code, such as a new class, rather than editing code that already works.
example: Adding a Triangle class without touching Circle or Square follows OCP.

definition: The L in SOLID, from Barbara Liskov (1987) and later Liskov and Wing: code written against a type must keep working when given any of its subtypes. A subtype must keep the parent's behavioural contract, not just match its method signatures.
example: A mutable Square that changes its height when you set its width breaks LSP for code expecting a Rectangle.

definition: The I in SOLID: no client should be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, role-based interfaces to one large one.
example: Splitting a Machine interface into Printer and Scanner lets a basic printer implement only print.

definition: The D in SOLID: high-level policy code and low-level detail code should both depend on abstractions, and the abstraction is owned by the high-level side. It is a rule about which way source-code dependencies point, not a technique for wiring objects.
example: An InvoiceService that depends on an InvoiceRepo protocol, implemented by PostgresRepo, follows DIP.

definition: A technique where an object receives the things it depends on (through its constructor or a parameter) instead of creating them itself. It makes substitution and testing easier, but on its own it does not invert dependency direction.
example: Passing a FakeMailer into Signup(mailer=...) in a test is dependency injection.

definition: A library that creates objects and wires their dependencies together automatically, such as Spring or Guice for Java. Useful in large codebases, but never required: plain constructor arguments do the same job.

"Don't repeat yourself", from Hunt and Thomas's The Pragmatic Programmer (1999): every piece of knowledge should have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation in a system. It targets duplicated knowledge, not code that merely looks similar.
example: One MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH constant used by sign-up and reset follows DRY.

definition: "Keep it simple, stupid": a design principle associated with the aircraft engineer Kelly Johnson. In software it means fewer concepts and fewer interactions for a reader to hold in their head, not the fewest lines.
example: A plain loop is often more KISS than a one-line nested comprehension.

definition: "You aren't gonna need it", from Extreme Programming: don't build a capability until you actually need it. It applies to speculative features, not to tests, refactoring or decisions that are costly to reverse later.
example: Building only CSV export when only CSV was asked for follows YAGNI.

definition: A design guideline, "only talk to your immediate friends": a method should call methods on itself, its parameters, objects it creates and its own fields, not on objects returned by those. It limits how much one piece of code knows about the structure of others.
example: order.shipping_city() follows it; order.customer.address.city breaks it.

definition: A long chain of calls or attribute accesses through several objects, such as a.b.c.d. It couples the caller to every class in the chain and usually breaks the Law of Demeter.
example: city = order.customer.address.city

definition: A guideline: instead of extracting data from an object to make a decision about it, tell the object what you want and let it decide. The rule then lives next to the data it protects.
example: acct.withdraw(amount) instead of checking acct.balance and subtracting yourself.

definition: Bertrand Meyer's rule that a function should either change state (a command) or return information without side effects (a query), not both. It makes calls safe to repeat when they look like questions.
example: has_stock(item, 2) ought to leave stock alone.

definition: In command-query separation, a function that changes state, such as saving, sending or mutating an object. It may return nothing, or a value that is not a fresh answer about the system.
example: reserve(item, qty) is a command.

definition: In command-query separation, a function that returns information and has no observable side effects, so calling it twice is the same as calling it once.
example: is_valid(order) should be a query.

definition: A design rule: a component should behave the way most users would expect, so similar operations behave similarly. Surprising behaviour causes misuse.
example: If list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, sorted() returning a new list ought to leave its input unchanged.

aliases: be liberal in what you accept
definition: Jon Postel's guideline for early internet protocols: be conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept. RFC 9413 (2023) argues that unchecked tolerance becomes a hidden obligation and can hide bugs and security holes.
example: Silently accepting a misspelt JSON field is the robustness principle at work.

definition: An observation by Hyrum Wright at Google: with enough users of an API, every observable behaviour of the system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the documentation promises. So any visible change can break someone.
example: Results that always happened to come back sorted get relied on, even though the docs said "no particular order".

definition: Robert C. Martin's package principle: depend in the direction of stability. A module should depend only on modules that are more stable (lower instability) than itself, so widely used code is not dragged along by code that changes often.
example: A core domain package (instability 0.1) importing a reporting package (instability 0.9) breaks it.

definition: A refactoring heuristic attributed to Don Roberts: write it the first time, duplicate it the second time, and extract a shared abstraction the third time, when you can see what really varies.

Sandi Metz's term for a shared function or class that no longer fits its callers, so it grows flags and branches for each one. She argues duplication is far cheaper; the fix is to inline it back into the callers and start again.
example: An export() helper with legacy, eu and for_finance flags is a wrong abstraction.

definition: Code that looks identical but represents different knowledge that will change for different reasons. Merging it couples unrelated rules, so it is not a DRY violation.
example: VAT at 20 % and a staff discount at 20 % are accidental duplication.

aliases: Kent Beck's rules of simple design
definition: Kent Beck's four rules, in Fowler's presentation: a simple design passes the tests, reveals intention, has no duplication and has the fewest elements. Correctness comes first and minimising elements last.

aliases: simple is not the same as easy
definition: A distinction from Rich Hickey's 2011 talk Simple Made Easy: simple means not intertwined (few parts, each doing one thing), while easy means familiar or close at hand. A heavyweight framework can be easy but not simple.
An agile software method developed by Kent Beck in the late 1990s. It emphasises tests written first, pair programming, small releases, continuous refactoring and simple design; YAGNI comes from it.
Fowler's term for a capability built now because you think you'll need it later. Even when the guess is right it carries a cost of delay and a cost of carry.
In Fowler's YAGNI analysis, the analysis, coding and testing effort spent building a presumptive feature now, wasted entirely if the feature is never needed.
In Fowler's YAGNI analysis, the value lost because other features shipped later while you built a presumptive feature.
In Fowler's YAGNI analysis, the ongoing extra effort the unused code adds to every change, test and review until it is needed.

In Fowler's YAGNI analysis, the rework needed when a presumptive feature turns out to have been built the wrong way, because the team only later learns what it should do. Fowler calls this technical debt.

Martin Fowler's proposal that investing in good internal design slows you down at first but lets you keep adding features faster later. He presents it as a hypothesis and judgement, not a measured result.
A design rule: shape your types so that invalid combinations of data cannot be built at all, instead of checking for them everywhere. Separate types for each state are a common way to do it.
example: A PaidOrder type that always has paid_at, instead of an Order whose status says paid while paid_at is None.

definition: The choice that stays correct and safe when nobody has thought harder about it. For a setting, a default chosen so that a caller who never touches it still gets correct, safe behaviour, such as certificate checks on and a finite timeout.
example: Python's requests library has no default timeout, which is not a safe default.

definition: A way to change an interface without breaking callers: add the new form alongside the old (expand), migrate every caller, then remove the old form (contract).
example: Add a new event field, move consumers over to it, then stop sending the old one.

definition: Detect bad input or a broken assumption as early as possible, usually where data enters the system, and stop with a clear error there. A failure close to its cause is cheap to diagnose.
example: Rejecting quantity -3 in the HTTP handler instead of letting it reach the database.

definition: How much one module depends on another: how much each must know about the other, so how likely a change in one forces a change in the other. The usual aim is low coupling.
example: Code that pokes another class's private list is tightly coupled to it.

definition: How closely the things inside one module belong together. High cohesion means a module has one clear purpose, so related changes happen in one place.
example: A billing module whose functions all serve billing rules is highly cohesive.

definition: The tightest kind of coupling: one module reaches into another's internal details, such as its private fields, so any internal change breaks it.
example: order._items.append(item)

definition: Coupling where several modules share global mutable data, so a change made by one silently affects the others.
example: Several modules writing CONFIG["currency"].

definition: Coupling where modules share an externally imposed format, protocol or device, so they must change together if that external thing changes.
example: Two modules that both parse the same vendor file layout.

definition: Coupling where one module passes a mode or flag value that steers the other's internal logic, so the caller must know how the callee works inside.
example: report(data, mode="summary")

definition: Coupling where a module is passed a whole record or object but uses only part of it. It ties the callee to the record's shape, though it can also let the signature stay stable.
example: greet(user) that only reads user.name.

definition: The loosest classic kind of coupling: modules share only the simple values they need, through parameters.
example: greet(name)

definition: Coupling where things must happen in a particular order or at a particular time, such as calling open() before read(). It is often invisible in the code's interfaces.
Coupling through an agreement that is not written in either module's interface, such as both assuming times are in UTC. Changing one side breaks the other without a compile error.
example: Two services that both 'know' status 3 means cancelled.

definition: The weakest cohesion: parts are grouped for no real reason, as in a utils.py of unrelated helpers.
example: slugify, retry and parse_vat_number in one helpers.py.

definition: Cohesion where parts are grouped because they are the same category of thing, even though they do different jobs.
example: A models/ folder holding every model in the app.

definition: Cohesion where parts are grouped because they run at the same time, such as everything done at start-up.
example: A startup() that opens the database, warms caches and sends a metric.

definition: Cohesion where parts are grouped because they run in a fixed sequence, even if they don't share data.
Cohesion where parts are grouped because they operate on the same data.
Cohesion where the output of one part is the input of the next, like stages of a pipeline.
The strongest classic cohesion: every part contributes to one well-defined task.
example: A module that only parses and validates VAT numbers.

definition: A software design method from the late 1960s and 1970s by Larry Constantine and colleagues, published by Stevens, Myers and Constantine (1974) and in Yourdon and Constantine's book Structured Design (1979). It introduced coupling and cohesion as measures of a good module structure.

Meilir Page-Jones's term ("born together"): two pieces of code are connascent if changing one forces a change in the other to keep the system correct. Its strength (from name up to identity), locality (how far apart the pieces are) and degree (how many pieces are involved) say how risky it is.
example: A caller passing arguments by position is connascent with the function's parameter order.

definition: The weakest form of connascence: both sides must agree only on a name, such as a function or keyword-argument name.
example: make_user(first="Ada") depends only on the name first.

definition: Connascence where both sides must agree on the type of a value.
Connascence where both sides must agree on what a particular value means, such as 3 meaning cancelled. Replacing the value with a named constant weakens it to connascence of name.
Connascence where both sides must agree on an order, such as the order of positional arguments or tuple fields.
example: make_user("Ada", "Lovelace", 36, True)

definition: Connascence where both sides must use the same algorithm, such as the same checksum or hash on client and server.
Dynamic connascence where things must happen in a particular order, such as open() before read().
Dynamic connascence where the timing of operations matters, such as a race between two threads.
Dynamic connascence where several values must change together to stay consistent.
Dynamic connascence where several components must reference the same object, not just equal ones.

Static connascence can be seen by reading the source code (name, type, meaning, position, algorithm). Dynamic connascence appears only at runtime (execution order, timing, value, identity) and is generally stronger.
A surface sign in code that often points to a deeper design problem, such as one change requiring edits in many files. A smell is a prompt to look closer, not proof of a bug.
example: Feature envy and shotgun surgery are code smells.

definition: A code smell where one logical change needs small edits in many modules, because related knowledge is scattered.
example: Adding a currency touches nine files in five modules.

definition: A code smell where one module changes for many unrelated reasons, a sign of low cohesion. It is the mirror image of shotgun surgery.
A code smell where a method uses another object's data more than its own, suggesting it belongs on that other object.
example: can_ship(order) that only inspects order.customer's fields.

definition: A code smell where two classes reach into each other's private parts, so neither can change alone.
A code smell of using raw strings and numbers where a small dedicated type would carry meaning and rules.
example: Storing money as a float and a currency string instead of a Money type.

definition: Lack of cohesion of methods: a family of metrics that measure how far a class's methods use non-overlapping groups of its fields. A high value suggests the class holds several concepts.
example: A class whose newsletter methods use only name and email, and whose billing methods use only card fields, scores badly.

definition: The number of other modules (or classes) that depend on a module: its incoming dependencies, written Ca in Robert C. Martin's metrics. High afferent coupling makes a module costly to change.
example: A module imported by 6 others has afferent coupling 6.

definition: The number of other modules (or classes) a module depends on: its outgoing dependencies, written Ce in Robert C. Martin's metrics.
example: A module that imports 2 others has efferent coupling 2.

definition: Robert C. Martin's metric: outgoing dependencies divided by all dependencies (efferent over afferent plus efferent), from 0 (stable, many depend on it) to 1 (unstable, it depends on others and nothing depends on it). It measures structure, not how often code actually changes.
example: 6 incoming and 2 outgoing gives 2 / 8 = 0.25.

definition: Robert C. Martin's set of numbers for judging a package's dependencies, including afferent and efferent coupling, instability and abstractness.
A system split into separate services that are still so tightly coupled they must be changed and deployed together. You pay the cost of a network without gaining independent deployment.
example: Eight services that must all redeploy when one shared model changes.

definition: A component that delivers events from publishers to whichever subscribers have registered, so senders don't know who receives. It loosens coupling but makes flow harder to trace.
An API designed so calls can be chained, each returning an object to call the next method on, reading almost like a sentence.
example: query.filter(...).order_by(...)

definition: A catch-all file such as utils.py or helpers.py for functions with no obvious home. It tends towards coincidental cohesion.
Code that a competent colleague who has never seen it can understand quickly and change safely. The aim is a lower cost for the next change, not elegance for its own sake.
A bare literal in code whose meaning is not stated, such as 86400 or status 3. Replace it with a named constant or enum so readers know what it means and changes happen in one place.
example: MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS = 5 instead of a bare 5.

definition: A value given a descriptive name, by convention in capitals in Python, such as MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS = 5. It documents intent and gives one place to change the value.
A boolean parameter that switches what a function does. It makes call sites unreadable (render(doc, True)) and suggests the function does two jobs.
example: render_preview(doc) and render_print(doc) instead of render(doc, True).

definition: A small object that groups parameters which always travel together, so functions take one meaningful argument instead of several loose ones.
example: An Address object instead of street, city, postcode.

definition: A Python parameter that must be passed by name, never by position. Parameters after a bare * in the signature are keyword-only (PEP 3102).
example: def transfer(*, amount, src, dst) forces transfer(amount=100, src=42, dst=17).

definition: An argument passed by naming its parameter, such as timeout=10, so the call does not depend on parameter order.
An argument matched to a parameter by its position in the call. Several positional arguments of the same type are easy to swap by mistake.
example: transfer(100, 42, 17)

definition: An early check at the top of a function that returns or raises for a special case, so the main logic is not nested inside several ifs.
example: if order is None: return

definition: The normal flow through code when nothing goes wrong. Guard clauses leave it unindented at the bottom of a function.
A naming convention that encodes a variable's type in its name, such as strName. Modern style guides discourage it because types and editors already show this.
A word in a name that adds no meaning, such as data, info, manager or handle. UserData tells a reader nothing that User doesn't.
A function or boolean value that answers a yes/no question. Good predicate names read as questions: is_active, has_permission, can_delete.
A value that is either true or false (True or False in Python), named after the logician George Boole.

How much detail something deals with, from the big picture (high level) down to fine detail (low level). In code, business steps are high level and SQL strings and sockets low level; a function that stays at one level reads like a summary.
example: checkout() calling add_tax, orders.save and notifier.order_placed stays at one level.

definition: A simplified interface that hides details behind a name or type, so callers depend on what something does rather than how. Good abstractions capture something genuinely shared; wrong ones force unrelated cases together.
example: A Mailer protocol with send() is an abstraction over SendGrid or SMTP.

definition: Fowler's rule for function size: if you have to read a block of code to work out what it does, extract it into a function named after what it does.
example: is_overdue(invoice) instead of a date comparison inline.

definition: Splitting code into so many tiny functions that each just calls the next, forcing readers to jump around without learning anything from the names.

Any observable change a function makes beyond returning a value: modifying an argument or field, writing a file, printing, sending a message. Hidden side effects in query-looking functions are expensive bugs.
example: is_valid(order) that sets order.validated_at.

definition: Changing code's internal structure without changing its observable behaviour, to make it easier to understand and change. Behaviour fixes belong in a separate change.
example: Renaming x[2] to m.active is a refactoring; changing > 18 to >= 18 is not.

definition: Python Enhancement Proposal: a numbered design document that describes a new Python feature, convention or process, such as PEP 8 (style) or PEP 544 (protocols).
Python's official style guide for code layout, naming and comments. Most Python projects and linters follow it.
example: Constants in capitals: MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS.

definition: Python's docstring conventions: a one-line summary in the imperative mood, a blank line, then detail.
The US government's space agency. Its Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 through a units mismatch between two teams' software.
A NASA probe lost in 1999 when ground software reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while the navigation software expected newton seconds, so the craft flew far too close to Mars.
An imperial unit of impulse (force multiplied by the time it acts). One pound-force second is about 4.45 newton seconds.
The SI unit of impulse: a force of one newton acting for one second. About 0.225 pound-force seconds.
Python's type for a length of time, from the datetime module. It carries its unit with it, so timedelta(seconds=30) cannot be misread as milliseconds.
example: timedelta(days=1).total_seconds() is 86400.0.

definition: A Python decorator (from the dataclasses module) that generates __init__, __repr__ and an equality method (__eq__) from annotated fields, for classes that mainly hold data. frozen=True makes instances read-only.
example: @dataclass class Member: first: str; age: int

definition: A type with a fixed set of named values, such as Status.CANCELLED. In Python it comes from the enum module; IntEnum members are also integers.
example: Status.TRIAL_EXPIRED instead of 3.

definition: Python's compact syntax for building a list from a loop and an optional condition: [f(x) for x in xs if cond(x)]. Readable when short, cryptic when nested.
example: [x * x for x in nums]

definition: A small anonymous function written inline. In Python, lambda x: x + 1 is a function that adds one, limited to a single expression.
An expression that picks one of two values: in Python, a if condition else b.
A Python string prefixed with f whose {expressions} are evaluated and inserted, such as f"Hi {name}".
A table listing every combination of a set of conditions with the result for each. Writing one before restructuring conditionals catches behaviour changes.
The default output stream of a program, normally the terminal. print() in Python writes to it.
A document of agreed conventions for naming, layout and idioms in a language or codebase, such as PEP 8 or Google's Python style guide. Consistency with it matters more than personal preference.
A style of programming that organises code as objects combining data (fields) with the methods that act on it, typically using classes, inheritance and polymorphism.
In Robert C. Martin's single responsibility principle, a group of people (such as finance or operations) who might request a change to some code.
The trade-off between adding new data types and adding new operations. Classes with methods make new types cheap and new operations expensive; functions over a fixed set of types do the opposite.
example: Adding volume() to every Shape class versus adding a Triangle class.

definition: What a type promises about its behaviour, not just its signatures: the inputs it accepts (preconditions), what it guarantees afterwards (postconditions) and what always holds (invariants). Bertrand Meyer's design by contract makes these explicit.
example: Rectangle.setWidth promises the height is unchanged.

definition: Something that must be true before an operation is called, such as the amount being positive. A subtype may not strengthen (narrow) its parent's preconditions.
Something an operation guarantees is true after it finishes, such as the balance falling by exactly the amount. A subtype may not weaken its parent's postconditions.

A type that can be used where its parent type is expected, for example through inheritance (Square extends Rectangle) or by matching a protocol. Liskov substitution says it must also keep the parent's behaviour.
A mechanism where a class reuses and extends another class's code and type. Used just to share code, it often breaks substitutability; composition is usually safer.
Building an object from other objects it holds and delegates to, instead of inheriting from them. It keeps types independent and avoids Liskov violations.
example: An Employee that holds a Contact and a PayrollRecord.

definition: A mutable object can be changed after creation; an immutable one cannot, so operations return a new object instead. Immutability removes many substitution and sharing bugs.
example: Python lists are mutable; tuples are immutable.

definition: Creating an interface for every class (IUserService with a single UserServiceImpl) with no second implementation or isolation need, adding indirection without benefit.
A small interface describing one capability a client needs, such as Printer or Reader, instead of everything an implementation can do.
A large interface with many methods, forcing implementers and clients to depend on operations they don't use. The interface segregation principle splits it.
In Java, a type that declares methods a class promises to provide; a class must say implements Printer to satisfy it (nominal typing).
example: class BasicPrinter implements Printer

definition: Python's way to declare an interface by shape (PEP 544): any class with matching methods satisfies it for a static type checker, without inheriting from it. It is not checked at runtime unless marked @runtime_checkable and tested with isinstance.
example: class SupportsRead(Protocol): def read(self, n: int) -> bytes: ...

definition: Type compatibility decided by shape: an object fits if it has the required members, whatever it inherits from. Python protocols and Go interfaces work this way.
Type compatibility decided by declared names: a class fits only if it explicitly inherits or implements the type, as with Java interfaces.
A tool, such as mypy or Pyright for Python, that reads type hints and reports type errors without running the code. Python itself ignores hints at runtime.
An annotation in Python code stating a variable's, parameter's or return value's expected type, such as email: str -> User | None. Checked by tools, not enforced by Python at runtime.
Types are attached to values and checked while the program runs, not before. Python is dynamically typed, so any object with the right attribute works at runtime.
The period while a program is executing, as opposed to when it is written or compiled. Some errors only appear at runtime.
An error reported by a compiler before the program runs, such as a type mismatch in Java. Behavioural mistakes like LSP violations usually don't produce one.
A function's name, parameters (with their types, if declared) and return type: what a caller sees without reading the body.
example: def find(users: list[User], email: str) -> User | None

definition: A stand-in object used in tests in place of a real dependency, such as a fake mailer that records messages instead of sending them.
Replacing a function, class or attribute at runtime, often in tests, without changing its source. Possible in Python but less explicit than injecting a dependency.
A design pattern that ensures a class has only one instance, shared globally. It controls how many instances exist, not which way dependencies point.
An object or function whose job is to create other objects, hiding which concrete class is built.
example: ExporterFactory().create("csv")

definition: A design pattern that keeps operations in separate visitor objects which handle each type in a fixed set of types. It makes adding operations cheap and adding types expensive.
Choosing code by the shape of a value. Python 3.10's match statement can destructure objects: case Add(a, b): ...
A design pattern that puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the caller can be given whichever one it needs.
A design where new features are added as separate modules that register with a core through a defined interface, without editing the core.
Code that sits between a request and its handler, such as logging or authentication, often as a chain where each step passes the request on.
Saving data so it outlives the program, typically in a database or file.
A class that hides how objects are stored and loaded behind methods like save and get, so business code doesn't depend on the database.
The Java Development Kit: the compiler, standard library and tools for writing Java programs.
example: Collections.unmodifiableList is part of the JDK.

definition: The Java Virtual Machine: the runtime that executes compiled Java bytecode. Kotlin and Scala also run on it.
Java's documentation comments and the tool that turns them into reference pages. The List Javadoc marks add as an optional operation.
A method in a Java collection interface that an implementation may refuse by throwing UnsupportedOperationException. It weakens what the interface really guarantees.
A Java method that returns a read-only view of a list. It has type List, but its add, remove, set and clear throw UnsupportedOperationException.

Signalling an error by raising an exception object, which travels up the call stack until a matching handler catches it. Used by Python, Java and C#; the error path is separate from normal return values.

An approach where failure is part of a function's return value instead of an exception, as with Go's (value, err) pair or Rust's Result<T, E>. Every failure point is visible, at the cost of more code.
example: f, err := os.Open(path)

definition: In Java, an exception that the compiler forces code to catch or declare with throws, such as IOException. Oracle's guideline: use them for conditions a caller can reasonably recover from.
example: String readString(Path p) throws IOException

definition: In Java, an exception (a RuntimeException or Error subclass) that need not be declared or caught. Oracle's guideline: use them for programming errors such as a null argument.
The report Python prints for an uncaught exception: the chain of calls that led to it, innermost last, plus the exception type and message. Chained exceptions show several.
The record of active function calls: each call adds a frame holding its local state, and returning removes it. Exceptions travel up the stack, and warnings' stacklevel picks a frame.

Linking a new exception to the one that caused it. In Python, raise X from e sets __cause__ ("direct cause", PEP 3134); raising inside an except without from records __context__ instead; raise X from None hides the original (added later by PEP 409 and PEP 415).
example: raise UserLookupFailed(uid) from e

definition: Python's error-handling statement: try runs code, except clauses handle matching exceptions, else runs if try finished normally, and finally always runs on the way out.
The part of a Python try statement that runs however the block exits, including by exception or return; used for cleanup. A return inside it discards any in-flight exception.
The part of a Python try statement that runs only when the try block completes normally, with no exception and no return, break or continue. Code there is not guarded by the except clauses.
An except: clause with no exception type. It catches BaseException, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, so it hides bugs and even stops Ctrl+C working.
Catching an exception and doing nothing useful with it (except: pass). The failure still happened; only the evidence is gone.
One place at the outer edge of a program or request that catches unexpected exceptions, logs them with their traceback once, and returns a generic error such as HTTP 500.
A Python object used with the with statement that runs set-up on entry and clean-up on exit, including when an exception occurs, such as closing a file or ending a transaction.
example: with open(path) as f: ...

aliases: easier to ask forgiveness than permission
definition: "Easier to ask forgiveness than permission": the Python style of attempting an operation and handling the exception if it fails, instead of checking first.
example: try: open(p) except FileNotFoundError: ...

definition: "Look before you leap": checking a condition before an operation (if os.path.exists(p): open(p)). With files and networks the check can be stale by the time of use.

aliases: time of check to time of use
definition: Time-of-check to time-of-use: a race condition where something changes between checking it and using it, such as a file deleted between exists() and open(). Also a class of security bug.
Fowler's validation pattern: collect every error into a list or object and return them together, instead of raising on the first one.
example: Returning ["email: invalid", "postcode: required"].

definition: A Python 3.11 exception that bundles several exceptions, handled with except*, for example when several concurrent tasks fail at once.
Python's standard library for concurrent code using async and await. A TaskGroup runs several tasks and raises an ExceptionGroup if any fail.
The standard, reference implementation of Python, written in C; the one you get from python.org.
The root of Python's exception hierarchy. Exception derives from it, but so do KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, which is why catching BaseException is dangerous.
The Python exception raised when the user presses Ctrl+C. It derives from BaseException, not Exception.
The Python exception raised by sys.exit() to stop the program. It derives from BaseException.
The Python exception raised when an object has no attribute of the requested name, such as None.name.
The Python exception for an argument of the right type but an unacceptable value, such as int("x").
The Python exception for an operation on the wrong type, or a call with the wrong arguments.
example: transfer(100) when amount is keyword-only.

definition: The Python exception raised when a dictionary (or mapping) lookup uses a missing key.
The Python exception raised when code uses a name that isn't defined, often a typo.
The Python exception raised when a file or directory that was requested does not exist.
The Python exception raised when dividing by zero.
The Python exception raised when a system-level operation times out.
The Python exception an iterator raises to signal it has no more items; for loops catch it automatically.
The Python exception raised when code is not valid Python, before it runs.
A Python warning about dubious but legal syntax. From Python 3.14 it is emitted for return, break or continue in a finally block (PEP 765).
The Python warning category for features that will be removed. Hidden by default unless triggered by code in __main__ (PEP 565); test runners show it.
The Python warning category for deprecations aimed at end users of applications; shown by default.
A Java unchecked exception thrown when an object doesn't support a requested operation, such as add on an unmodifiable list.
A Java unchecked exception thrown when code uses null where an object is required.
A Java unchecked exception for an argument a method cannot accept.
Java's checked exception for input/output failures; FileNotFoundException is a subclass.
The Java base class for unchecked exceptions, used for programming errors.
A unique ID a client sends with a request so the server can recognise retries of the same logical operation and return the first result instead of repeating it, within the server's retention window.
example: Stripe accepts an Idempotency-Key header on charge requests.

definition: A retry strategy where the wait between attempts grows by a constant factor, usually doubling, so a struggling service gets more breathing room. Usually combined with a cap and jitter.
example: Waits of 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s.

definition: Random variation added to retry delays so that many clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry at the same moment.
A surge of synchronised retries from many clients that keeps a recovering service overloaded, turning a brief failure into an outage.
A limit on how long to wait for an operation. A timeout means you stopped waiting, not that the operation failed: it may still complete.
A failure caused by something outside the code that may clear up by itself, such as a network blip or a busy server. Often handled by retrying with backoff.
Code that runs very often, so its speed matters to overall performance.
A widely used online payments provider with an HTTP API for charging cards, sending webhooks and handling refunds.
Detecting repeated copies of the same data, message or request and keeping or processing only one, usually by comparing a unique identifier or a content hash.

A Rust attribute that makes the compiler warn (through the unused_must_use lint) when a value such as a Result is ignored. By default it is a warning, not an error, though a project can deny the lint.
A tool that scans source code for likely mistakes and style problems without running it, such as Ruff or Pylint for Python.
Safe to use from several threads at once without corrupting data or giving wrong results.
A function the operating system calls asynchronously when the process receives a signal, such as SIGINT from Ctrl+C. Only limited operations are safe inside one.

The rules of the problem the software serves, such as how refunds or overtime work, as opposed to technical plumbing like HTTP handling or storage code. A business rule can still be enforced by the database, for example with a constraint.
example: "Insufficient funds" is a domain outcome for a bank.

definition: A string literal as the first statement of a Python module, class or function that documents it for callers; tools like help() and IDEs show it. PEP 257 sets the conventions.
The grammatical form of a command: "Return the total", "Fix rounding". Used for docstring summaries and commit subject lines.
One of the common layouts for Python docstrings, with Args:, Returns: and Raises: sections. NumPy and reStructuredText styles are alternatives; pick one per project.
A plain-text markup language used for Python documentation; Sphinx reads it, and one common docstring style uses its field syntax such as :param x:.
A documentation generator widely used for Python projects, which builds HTML or PDF docs from reStructuredText and docstrings.
Anything in Python that can be called with (), such as a function, method or object with __call__.
A documentation framework that separates four kinds of docs by the reader's need: tutorials (learning), how-to guides (doing a task), reference (looking up facts) and explanation (understanding).
In Diátaxis, a lesson that teaches a newcomer by doing, step by step, such as "Build your first app".
In Diátaxis, steps for solving one practical task, such as "Rotate API keys", without background theory.
In Diátaxis, dry, complete technical descriptions to look things up in, such as function signatures and endpoints.
In Diátaxis, discussion that helps the reader understand why, such as design background or how caching works.
The introductory file at the top of a project, usually README.md: what it is, how to install it and a quick working example.
A comment marking unfinished work. Useful only with a description and an owner or ticket so it can be found and finished.
example: # TODO(PAY-311): handle refunds

definition: The most widely used version control system: it records snapshots of a project as commits and lets people branch, merge and review history.
A saved snapshot of changes in Git, with an author, a timestamp and a message explaining it. Each commit should hold one logical change.
The text attached to a commit: a short imperative subject (about 50 characters), a blank line, then a body wrapped at about 72 characters explaining what and why.
example: Cap retry backoff at 30s

definition: A Git command that shows, for each line of a file, the commit and author that last changed it, so you can find the message explaining it.
A Git command that lists commits; --oneline shows just each commit's short ID and subject line.
A Git command that binary-searches history to find the commit that introduced a bug. Small, single-purpose commits make it far more useful.
The line-by-line differences between two versions of code, as shown in code review or by git diff.
The parts of a library, service or module that outside code is allowed to use. Callers you can't see depend on it, so changing it is costly.
Software development kit: a library and tools for using a platform or service from code, such as a payment provider's Python SDK.
A version scheme MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible features and PATCH for backwards-compatible fixes. Versions 0.y.z are unstable.
example: 2.4.1 → 3.0.0 after adding a required parameter.

definition: In semantic versioning, the first number; incremented for incompatible API changes, resetting MINOR and PATCH to 0.
In semantic versioning, the middle number; incremented for new backwards-compatible features, resetting PATCH to 0.
In semantic versioning, the last number; incremented for backwards-compatible bug fixes.
A semantic version with a hyphenated suffix such as 3.0.0-rc.1, marking an unstable build before the release.
A change that leaves existing callers working without modification.
example: Adding an optional parameter with a default.

definition: A change that makes existing callers fail or behave differently, such as removing a function or adding a required parameter.
Marking a feature as scheduled for removal, usually with a warning, so users have time to move off it before it goes.

A parameter of Python's warnings.warn that chooses which call-stack frame a warning is reported against: 1 (the default) points at the line that calls warn, 2 at the caller of the function containing that line.
A Python setting that decides whether each warning is ignored, shown or turned into an error, set with -W, PYTHONWARNINGS or warnings.simplefilter.
The name Python gives the module run directly (python app.py), as opposed to imported modules.
Request for Comments: a numbered document published by the RFC Editor, mostly from the IETF, that defines or discusses internet standards and practices.
"Maintaining Robust Protocols" (2023): an informational RFC arguing that silently tolerating bad input creates hidden obligations, and that protocols should address deviations actively.

A formal description of the fields and types in messages or events, written in a schema language such as JSON Schema, Apache Avro or Google's Protocol Buffers, so producers and consumers share an explicit, versionable contract.
The defined structure of data: tables and columns in a database, or fields and types in a message format.
The exact byte or text layout of data sent between systems. Once others depend on it, changing it needs versioning and coordination.
A specific URL and method in an HTTP API that clients call, such as POST /orders.
Value-added tax: a consumption tax added to the price of goods and services, set by government; the UK standard rate is 20 %.
Human resources: the part of a business that handles staff, pay policies and benefits.
Information technology: here, the team responsible for an organisation's systems and databases.
Database administrator: the person responsible for a database's schema, performance, backups and security.
Data transfer object: a simple object that only carries data across a boundary, such as between services, with no behaviour.
Object-relational mapping: a library that maps database tables to classes so code works with objects instead of SQL, such as SQLAlchemy or Django's ORM.
A human-readable data format often used for configuration files, based on indentation.
Comma-separated values: a plain-text table format, one row per line and columns separated by commas.
Extensible Markup Language: a text format for structured data using nested tags.
A column-oriented file format for large data sets, common in analytics.
Portable Document Format: a fixed-layout document file format.
Command-line interface: a program you use by typing commands in a terminal.
Integrated development environment: a code editor with tools such as autocomplete, refactoring and a debugger, like VS Code or PyCharm.
Coordinated Universal Time: the world's reference time standard, with no time zone offset or daylight saving.
The international standard for writing dates and times, such as 2026-10-10T14:30:00Z.
A standard machine-readable format for describing HTTP APIs, from which docs and client code can be generated.
A small SQL database engine stored in a single file and embedded in the program; Python includes it as sqlite3.
A small value computed from data to detect accidental changes; both sides must use the same algorithm and encoding.
The number of digits after the decimal point; "2 dp" means rounded to hundredths.
The smallest named division of a currency and how many decimal places it uses: 2 for pounds (pence), 0 for yen.
A tight bound on growth: Θ(g(n)) means the cost grows in proportion to g(n), ignoring constant factors and small inputs. Θ(n²) means doubling n roughly quadruples the work.
A lower bound on growth: Ω(g(n)) means the cost grows at least in proportion to g(n) for large inputs.
How the running time of an algorithm grows as the input size n grows, usually written with Big-O.
Lockheed Martin's advanced aircraft development division, founded in 1943 and long led by Kelly Johnson, with whom the KISS principle is associated.
A Python function that returns whether a path exists right now. The answer can be stale by the time you open the file.
